long_biography.plain_text:
MidFirst grew out of the mortgage business created by George J. Records. His son joined the organization, became vice chair and took the chair and chief executive posts in 1998. Under his direction, the Oklahoma institution developed from a regional lender into a national banking business, giving him an active record of stewardship beyond the advantage of succession.

Records handed day-to-day executive authority to Todd Dobson in 2025 but retained the chair. Federal Reserve notices show control flowing through Midland Financial and multiple Records family trusts, several named for him. Those arrangements connect him economically to the group without revealing a precise personal percentage or sole ownership. They also do not turn customer deposits, loan portfolios, liquidity or regulatory capital into private holdings. His durable business position combines a financial platform received from the previous generation with the value added during his long management tenure.

uncertainties.detail: The Federal Reserve spells the full name George Jeffrey Records, Jr. MidFirst uses G. Jeffrey Records, Jr. and Jeff Records for the same banker. The proposed detail fields normalize George as first name, Jeffrey as middle name and Jr. as suffix.

MidFirst's current leadership page identifies Records as chairman and Todd Dobson as chief executive. The 2025 transition announcement confirms Records remained chairman after relinquishing the chief executive role.

Federal Reserve records establish indirect voting control through Midland Financial and a network of Records family trusts, including trusts named for G. Jeffrey Records, Jr. They do not disclose his exact personal economic percentage or support describing him as sole owner.

Succession from his father establishes an inherited family platform, while his decades of executive leadership and documented expansion establish active development rather than passive inheritance alone.

MidFirst's loans, deposits, liquidity, regulatory capital, earnings and balance-sheet assets belong to the bank. Trust-based voting control does not make those gross corporate resources Records's personal property or net worth.
